comparison: Both address the exploratory analysis of different switch types (C56-C58). OpenEval finds these results supportive but notes they are exploratory and need caution. Peer reviewers are more critical, indicating the analysis may be insufficient and requesting more detailed examination of specific category switches, suggesting current analysis doesn't provide adequate leverage on mechanisms.

Both discuss the Andrews-Hanna framework and differential patterns between univariate/multivariate results (C84-C87). OpenEval finds this comparison appropriate and well-supported. Peer reviewers also accept the correspondence with the framework but recommend removing speculation about MVPA differences, limiting interpretive claims.

Both evaluate MVPA findings showing differential encoding across DMN sub-networks (C4, C37, C60-C63, C90). OpenEval finds these well-supported and notes MVPA's greater sensitivity. Peer reviewers are more skeptical, viewing MVPA as 'useful confirmation but not much more,' noting differences are 'basically uninterpretable' and that other regions might also discriminate tasks, thus limiting interpretive value.

Both address speculation about resting-state DMN activity (C93-C96). OpenEval marks this as uncertain and appropriately speculative, noting both explanations are plausible but require additional data. Peer reviewers question whether DMN activations are necessarily transient and ask authors to address why previous DMN accounts (mind-wandering, introspection, social cognition) seem loosely related to task switching.

Both address behavioral RT findings (C39-C41). OpenEval finds these well-supported with appropriate statistics showing graded RT pattern. Peer reviewers also do not challenge the behavioral findings, acknowledging RT differences as part of experimental design and addressing them as potential confounds in MVPA.

Both evaluate the core theoretical interpretation about DMN and cognitive context switching (C5, C28, C68, C71, C103, C105). OpenEval finds this well-supported by empirical findings, though notes the mechanism remains speculative. Peer reviewers fundamentally challenge this interpretation as UNSUPPORTED, stating results are 'in conflict' and that lack of similar-switch effects 'undercuts the notion' of context sensitivity, questioning whether context changes are truly larger than previous studies.

Both address univariate fMRI findings showing DMN activation patterns (C3, C36, C42-C48, C50-C51, C55, C69, C82). OpenEval finds these robustly supported with appropriate statistics and converging evidence, though notes lack of similar-switch activation is unexpected. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'robust DMN activations' and a 'well-done study' but raise major concerns about interpretation, questioning whether results reflect 'cognitive context' versus simply stimulus type changes.

Both address the unexpected lack of similar-switch effects and comparison to prior task-switching literature (C97-C102, C77-C79). OpenEval marks this as uncertain, noting authors appropriately acknowledge the finding and offer plausible explanations. Peer reviewers identify this as a 'major concern' and mark it UNSUPPORTED, stating the disparity with previous studies is problematic and that authors don't adequately explain why previous studies didn't activate DMN, requesting systematic comparison.

Both evaluate RT control analyses for MVPA (C65-C67). OpenEval finds these appropriate and strengthening confidence in MVPA results through converging evidence. Peer reviewers also do not challenge these control analyses, acknowledging they adequately address the RT confound methodological issue.

OpenEval R9 addresses comparison to prior literature and distinction in switch magnitude (C27, C77-C79), finding it supported though noting parametric manipulation would strengthen claims. Peer R8 overlaps partially but focuses more broadly on the disparity with previous task-switching studies (C77-C79, C98-C102), marking this UNSUPPORTED and requesting systematic comparison and literature review.

OpenEval R3 addresses broad univariate findings including main effects and interactions (C46, C49, C52 among others). Peer R2 specifically challenges the lack of similar-switch effects (C46, C49, C52, C97), stating this 'undercuts' the cognitive context interpretation and that labeling 'obfuscates' the distinction between question changes versus stimulus type changes.

OpenEval evaluates mechanistic interpretations about task structure and attentional processes (C72-C76) as uncertain and explicitly speculative, requiring additional experimental evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific mechanistic claims.

OpenEval evaluates the connection to memory literature and context processing (C80-C83) as supported with appropriate citations, though somewhat speculative without direct memory manipulations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these memory-related claims.

OpenEval evaluates interpretation of task differences and stronger decoding of dissimilar tasks (C88-C89, C91) as supported and consistent with hypothesis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific decoding interpretation claims.

OpenEval evaluates experimental design and methodology (C29-C34, C106-C118) as supported with adequate detail, reasonable sample size, and well-balanced task design. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing methodological design claims.

OpenEval evaluates background claims and literature context (C1-C2, C6-C26) as supported with appropriate citations representing established knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for background literature claims.

OpenEval evaluates ROI definition method (C119) as supported using standard approach from seminal paper, though notes some circularity. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for ROI definition methodology.
